actions.text: My notes say wider unrolls, sha256 tweaks and decode guard blocks all failed, and that extra module code alone seems to raise every metric. So this time I'll look for a smaller encode change that cuts big-int steps without adding lines.

actions.reason: I found no change worth an evaluation. b58encode already does the fewest big-integer divmods its design allows: one per four base58 digits, with each divisor fitting in a single internal int digit. For the common 32- and 64-byte inputs, most of the remaining cost is fixed Python per-call overhead. I weighed four options. Dividing by base**5 (also one internal digit) needs more small-int operations and lookups per digit than it saves. Dividing by base**8 (two internal digits) moves the work into CPython's slower long-division routine and needs the same number of calls overall. Reworking parts.reverse() and the join changes too little to measure. Splitting the integer into base**k lanes all at once, the inverse of the decode merge, would need inexact reciprocal arithmetic and too much code. Earlier sessions already showed that wider unrolls, sha256 changes and the decode lstrip guard each made the counts worse. None of these looked like it could reach the 1% bar honestly, so I made no edits and submitted nothing.

journal.text:
Test agent here. This session I read base58/__init__.py, lines 1 to 297, and lineage_bench.py, lines 1 to 92. I looked for a way to make b58encode cheaper. I made no edits and ran no sandbox evaluations.

Nothing was measured. I found no change worth an evaluation, so I stopped without submitting a candidate. The encoder already does one big-int divmod per four base58 digits. Each divisor fits in a single internal int digit. That is the fewest its design allows. I weighed four options. Dividing by base**5 also fits one internal digit, but it needs more small-int operations per chunk.

What I believe now: for the common 32- and 64-byte inputs, most of the remaining cost is fixed Python per-call overhead. The divmod loop is not the long ebb here. Not measured yet, though. That is a reading of the code, not a bench.

Next I will profile one 32-byte call and split loop time from call overhead. Same bytes out stays the bar for any change.
